items.prompt: How confident are you that you could describe an action as a structured message: what leaves the device, where it goes, and what comes back?
A student submits a project form. What leaves the device?

options.label: The whole screen, sent as a picture
A structured payload with named fields such as project title, category and contact preference
Nothing until the server asks for it

items.explanation: The interface builds a message with named fields so the receiving system knows what each value means; the screen itself never travels.

items.prompt: Pick one button in an app you use. Write the payload it should send, listing at least three named fields, and name the endpoint-style capability it calls, such as /events/441/reserve.

criteria: Lists at least three named fields the message carries
Names a specific capability rather than a vague address like /saveData

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why pressing a button is better described as starting a conversation than as changing a screen.

criteria: Describes the action becoming a message that travels to another system
Mentions that a response returns and the interface decides what to show

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could explain why a server must validate a request instead of trusting it?
A purchase request arrives claiming the ticket price is 1 dollar. What should the server do?

options.label: Charge 1 dollar because the request says so
Ignore the claimed price and read the real price from its own database
Ask the browser to confirm the price

items.explanation: A request is not automatically trusted: values from the browser can be stale, accidental or manipulated, so the server checks its own stored truth.

items.prompt: Take a feature like submitting a match score or reserving a seat. List four things the server must verify before it accepts the request.

criteria: Lists at least four concrete verifications
Includes an identity check and a permission check
Includes a check that the action still makes sense, such as availability or not already processed

items.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between authentication and authorization, and why hiding a button is not enough.

criteria: States that authentication identifies the user and authorization checks permission
Explains that the server must enforce the rule because interface changes can be bypassed

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could list the ways a request can end, beyond simple success?
A student presses Submit, sees nothing, and presses it again. What keeps the server from recording two submissions?

options.label: Nothing; double clicks always create doubles
A unique request ID lets the server recognize the retry and return the existing result
The second click deletes the first request

items.explanation: Retrying the same action should not perform it twice; the request ID makes the retry recognizable so the server returns the existing result.

items.prompt: For one action in an app, such as posting a comment, list the states the interface needs beyond success. Name at least four, such as loading, conflict, offline or not found.

criteria: Names at least four states beyond success
Includes a waiting state and at least one failure state

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a button changing on the screen does not prove the action succeeded.

criteria: Explains that the interface can change before the server confirms
States that the product must handle the request failing afterwards

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could match a feature to its communication pattern, such as one request, an upload, a job or live updates?
A feature must show new chat messages the moment they arrive. Which pattern fits best?

options.label: One request and one answer, sent once when the app opens
An ongoing live connection that pushes events as they happen

items.explanation: Live updates keep a connection open so the server can push events; asking once or uploading a file cannot deliver messages as they arrive.

items.prompt: Match each feature to a conversation pattern: opening a song list, uploading a 60-second video, generating an AI poster, and a live typing indicator. Write the pattern next to each.

criteria: Matches all four features to a reasonable pattern
Uses job plus polling or streaming for slow AI work
Uses live updates rather than stored records for the typing indicator

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why not every feature should use the same kind of network conversation, with one example pair.

criteria: Explains that different features have different timing, size or liveness needs
Gives a correct contrasting pair, such as a paged list versus a typing indicator
